about.title: About Genesis
about.lead: Genesis is the digital companion to an educational board game for learning astronomy and calendars.
about.gameBody: Genesis shows how the Sun, the Earth and the Moon move together, and how that movement shapes both the Gregorian and the Hebrew calendars. Children and adults can explore the seasons, the months and the phases of the Moon through play.
about.try1: Enter your birthday and discover your Hebrew birthday.
about.try2: See the phase of the Moon on any night.
about.try3: Travel through days, months and years and watch the two calendars move against each other.
about.creatorBody: Genesis was born in the imagination of a woman who loves the night sky and the stories that calendars tell. It began as an educational board game, made to bring children and families together around a table to learn about the Sun, the Moon and time itself.
about.creatorBody2: But the real heart of Genesis is its creator. She is one of the kindest people you could ever meet: generous with her time, patient with every question, and always the first to lift others up. Wherever she goes, she makes the world a little brighter and a little better. Like the Moon that always returns, full and shining, her kindness never runs out. We could all learn from her.
about.creatorThanks: Thank you for every star you have helped us see.

phaseInfo.newMoon: The Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us. A new Hebrew month begins with the new Moon, and its first day is called Rosh Chodesh, the head of the month.
phaseInfo.waxingCrescent: A thin silver curve appears in the west just after sunset. In ancient Jerusalem, people who saw this first sliver told the court, and the new month was declared.
phaseInfo.firstQuarter: Half of the Moon looks lit, but it has travelled only a quarter of the way around the Earth. It rises around noon and sets around midnight.
phaseInfo.waxingGibbous: Gibbous means hump-backed. Each evening the Moon rises about 50 minutes later than the night before as it grows towards full.
phaseInfo.fullMoon: The Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so we see the Moon's whole lit face. Passover and Sukkot begin on the 15th of their months, so they are always celebrated under a full Moon.
phaseInfo.waningGibbous: The Moon now rises after sunset and shrinks a little every night. It always shows us the same face, because it turns once on its axis for every trip around the Earth.
phaseInfo.lastQuarter: The other half of the Moon is lit now. It rises around midnight and is still high in the sky at sunrise, so look for it in the morning.
phaseInfo.waningCrescent: A thin crescent rises just before dawn. Soon the Moon disappears in the Sun's glare, and a new Hebrew month is about to begin.

monthInfo.tishrei: The year begins with Rosh Hashanah on the 1st, followed by Yom Kippur on the 10th and Sukkot under the full Moon of the 15th.
monthInfo.cheshvan: Also called Marcheshvan. It is the only month without festivals, and it can have 29 or 30 days, which helps the calendar adjust the length of the year.
monthInfo.kislev: Hanukkah begins on the 25th, near the darkest nights of the year, while the Moon is shrinking towards the new Moon.
monthInfo.tevet: Hanukkah ends in the first days of Tevet, in the middle of winter.
monthInfo.shvat: Tu BiShvat, the New Year of the Trees, falls on the 15th, under a full Moon, when almond trees begin to blossom in Israel.
monthInfo.adar: Purim is celebrated on the 14th, just before the full Moon. In leap years Adar is doubled into Adar I and Adar II.
monthInfo.adar1: Adar I is the extra month added in leap years, seven times every 19 years. It keeps the lunar calendar in step with the Sun, so Passover always stays in spring.
monthInfo.adar2: In leap years Purim is celebrated on the 14th of Adar II, one month before Passover.
monthInfo.nisan: The Torah calls Nisan the first of the months. Passover begins on the 15th, under the full Moon of spring.
monthInfo.iyyar: Lag BaOmer, a day of bonfires and celebration, falls on the 18th.
monthInfo.sivan: Shavuot, the festival of the giving of the Torah, is on the 6th, seven weeks after Passover.
monthInfo.tamuz: A summer month. The 17th of Tammuz begins three weeks of mourning that end on Tisha B'Av.
monthInfo.av: Tisha B'Av on the 9th is a day of mourning, while Tu B'Av on the 15th, under the full Moon, is a joyful day of love.
monthInfo.elul: The last month of the year, a time of reflection before Rosh Hashanah, when the shofar is blown.

quiz.title: Hebrew months quiz
quiz.intro: Five quick questions about the Hebrew months and the Moon. Every round brings new questions, and your progress is saved.
quiz.perfect: Perfect! You are a true star of the Hebrew calendar.
quiz.good: Great job! You know the sky well.
quiz.tryAgain: Good start! Play again to learn more.
quiz.explainDaysShorter: Twelve Moon months last about 354 days, about 11 days less than a solar year. So the Hebrew months slip about 11 days earlier each year, and every two or three years an extra month, Adar I, brings them back in step with the seasons.
